column4: After creating the human for trial, God says He showed him the road, then names its two responses, gratitude and disbelief; this is the closest parallel to the two visible ridges.
God inspires the soul with both its depravity and its wariness, restating the two disclosed moral directions without road vocabulary.
This ayah gives success as the end of one of the two possibilities named in 91:8: the one who purifies the soul succeeds.
This ayah gives failure as the other end of 91:8, so the two shown possibilities culminate in two outcomes as they do in the section.
The declaration that human striving is diverse opens the same divided road scene: bodies are moving, but their exertions head in unlike directions.
Giving and taqwa identify the active choice that 92:7 will ease toward ease, matching the costly acts that cross the pass.
Affirming the best completes the disposition of the giver in 92:5 before that traveler is eased along the easier end.
God's promise to ease the giver toward ease makes moral action a road one is fitted to travel.
Miserliness and imagined self-sufficiency identify the refusal corresponding to the man who will not undertake the pass.
Denying the best completes the miser's stance before 92:10 names the difficult destination to which he is eased.
Being eased toward hardship makes the avoided moral difficulty issue in another, ruinous difficulty.
His wealth cannot help when he tumbles down; the downward fall and useless property answer the section's unmade ascent and consumed wealth.
God states that guidance belongs to Him, confirming that the failure before the pass is not a failure to supply guidance.
The arrogant see the way of right and do not take it, but see the way of error and take it; visibility, two routes, and refusal all coincide with the image.
Thamud were guided but preferred blindness to guidance, making culpable preference rather than inability to find the road the decisive failure.
The person turned back on his heels after God's guidance wanders bewildered while companions call him toward guidance; heel-turning, perplexity, and the offered road meet in one scene.
The ayah contrasts one walking fallen on his face with one walking upright on a straight road, turning moral guidance into bodily posture and movement.
God assumes responsibility for directing the road while acknowledging that some roads deviate, a close counterpart to guidance that places distinct routes before the traveler.
Firm mountains contain broad passes as roads so that people may be guided; this supplies the literal mountain-road anatomy developed for the pass.
Mountains, rivers, and roads are placed in the earth so people can find their way, joining raised land to traversable routes.
Landmarks and stars complete 16:15's road scene by furnishing visible means through which travelers are guided.
Those who exert themselves for God are promised guidance into His ways, joining deliberate effort to further guidance rather than treating guidance as a substitute for effort.
True righteousness includes giving cherished wealth, freeing people, and patience in poverty, suffering, and danger—the same costly acts and endurance that constitute the pass.
Fear, hunger, and losses test the travelers, while the ayah commands good news for the patient; hunger-with-hardship and endurance are concrete features of the section.
The tested people of 2:155 hold their direction under affliction by locating both origin and return with God.
Those who endure the test receive mercy and are explicitly called the guided, linking patience under hardship to successful guidance.
The question whether believers expect to enter the Garden before striving and patience are manifested directly denies arrival without the difficult crossing.
The believers are asked whether they expect to enter the Garden without the severe distress and shaking suffered by earlier travelers; the destination lies beyond lived hardship.
Every human is laboring laboriously toward the Lord and will meet Him, turning unavoidable toil into directed travel with an encounter at its end.
The human has only what he strives for, so the road's result belongs to enacted exertion rather than merely seeing the route.
A person's striving will be seen, echoing the section's insistence that the decisive missing thing is the bodily act.
The fullest recompense for striving supplies the road's final return after the effort of 53:39-40.
Patience for the Lord's face, prayer, and spending secretly and openly culminate in عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ, joining endurance and expenditure to the road's good end.
Gardens and the entry of the righteous family supply the reached abode whose outcome 13:22 names and whose gates the angels enter.
The angels connect peace and the excellent عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ expressly to the travelers' patience.
The ayah names the two ends with the source section's root: the outcome of the wary is the Garden, while the outcome of the disbelievers is fire.
Perseverance in prayer, God's provision, and the statement that the outcome belongs to taqwa gather patient exertion, sustenance, and the road's end.
Moses tells his people to seek God's help and be patient, then declares that the earth's final outcome belongs to the wary.
Noah is commanded to be patient and is promised that the outcome belongs to the wary, pairing endurance on the way with its end.
Mutual counsel to truth and mutual counsel to patience exactly parallels the travelers' reciprocal counsel at the pass.
The command to hold oneself with those who call on their Lord enacts the source definition of patience as restraining the self rather than fleeing discomfort.
The layered command to be patient, outlast others, and remain stationed gives patience the bodily firmness required in a frightening passage.
At a terrifying encounter believers are told to stand firm and remember God, staging the self-possession that the section derives from patience.
The command not to quarrel and lose courage ends with patient endurance, showing how the travelers preserve strength while under pressure.
After commanding active moral work, Luqman tells his son to endure what befalls him and calls this a matter requiring resolve.
Refusing to lag behind is explained through thirst, fatigue, and hunger suffered on God's road, the same bodily cost gathered around ascent and masghaba.
Every expenditure and every valley crossed is credited, uniting spent wealth with actual passage through difficult terrain.
Both the affluent and the constrained must spend from what God gave; limited burden is followed by God's promise to make ease after hardship.
The command to fear God as far as one can, listen, obey, and spend joins bodily capacity, forward response, and victory over miserliness.
Those who spend for God's pleasure and inner firmness are compared to a garden on raised ground, bringing expenditure and literal elevation into one image.
The ayah distinguishes God's act of guidance from the believer's act of spending and says that good expenditure returns to the giver who seeks God's face.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, enact the expenditure cited beside patience and عُقْبَى ٱلدَّارِ in 13:22.
The good is not reached until one spends what one loves, making expenditure the costly threshold to be crossed.
The Helpers prefer others even while in privation, showing the pass's feeding and spending as an act undertaken from within one's own hardship.
Feeding the poor person, orphan, and captive despite love of the food closely restages the concrete deeds on the far side of the pass.
The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, locating the difficult act in its Godward intention.
Their fear of a grim, distressful day explains why present generosity is the meaningful difficult road rather than avoidance of all difficulty.
God protects the feeders from that day's evil and grants radiance and joy, supplying the result of their chosen act.
The Garden is explicitly their reward for patience, joining the completed acts of feeding to endurance and outcome.
The human is created anxious, providing the native condition from which patience must restrain the self.
When harm touches him he panics, precisely the جَزُوعًا response named in the section's definition of patience.
When good touches him he withholds, pairing panic before hardship with refusal to expend what the pass requires.
Those devoted to prayer are excepted from the panic-and-withholding pattern, opening the alternative course.
Constancy in prayer gives the alternative course the sustained discipline of a traveler who does not turn back.
The successful group recognizes a fixed right within its wealth, reversing possessive withholding.
That right belongs to the asker and the deprived, identifying the people whom expenditure must reach.
Failure to honor the orphan is one concrete refusal of the pass's demand.
Failure to urge one another to feed the poor reverses both feeding and the mutual moral counsel of the travelers.
Devouring inheritance greedily shows wealth moving into consumption rather than outward through the pass.
An excessive love of wealth identifies the attachment behind the refusals in 89:17-19.
Denial of recompense introduces the person whose treatment of the vulnerable displays refusal of the road and its end.
Driving away the orphan is the direct opposite of the pass's care for the nearby orphan.
Not urging the feeding of the poor reverses both the act and the reciprocal urging found in the section.
Withholding even small assistance condenses the bodily non-action behind refusal of the pass.
When commanded to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers refuse to feed those in need, a spoken rejection of the disclosed deed.
The condemned person's wealth has not benefited him, answering the boast about consumed wealth with its uselessness at the journey's end.
His authority has perished, placing the source root's destruction sense beside the collapse of worldly power.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is named among the causes of this ruined end.
The man assigned the forced ascent of 74:17 had first been given extensive wealth, matching the section's wealthy refuser.
God had smoothed life out for him, sharpening the irony that his refusal will culminate in a forced hard climb.
His demand for still more exposes appetite for increase rather than expenditure on the difficult good.
His stubborn opposition to God's signs identifies why the man of ease and wealth is assigned the ascent in 74:17.
The question of what brought the guilty into Saqar frames fire as the reached destination of a sequence of refusals.
The guilty confess that they did not feed the poor, explicitly carrying failure at the pass into the fire scene.
Heavy scales open the successful branch of the final two-way outcome.
A pleasing life is the reached end for the person whose scales are heavy.
Light scales open the opposite branch and immediately precede the downward destination in 101:9.
The neighbour identifies the abyss of 101:9 as a fiercely hot fire, completing the source section's fall-to-fire relation.
Transgression marks the first of two opposed human courses.
Preferring the nearer life identifies the choice that makes the easy-looking course end badly.
Hell is the abode of that first course, giving it a terminal destination.
The second person fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, enacting patience as self-restraint.
The Garden is the abode reached by the self-restraining course.
At the descent to earthly life God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither stray nor suffer, making response to prior guidance decisive.
Turning away from the reminder produces a constricted life and blind resurrection, the ruinous result of refusing the shown way.
The resurrected person asks why he is blind although he had been able to see, foregrounding the difference between incapacity and culpable refusal.
God answers that signs came and were abandoned, confirming that the person's blindness follows neglect of what had been shown.
The reminder is offered so that whoever wills may take a road to the Lord, stating the voluntary road image directly.
Human willing is placed within God's will, supplying the theological boundary around the choice in 76:29.
Mercy for whom God wills and painful punishment for wrongdoers give the chosen road its two ends.
Truth is disclosed, belief or disbelief is left as a choice, and the disbeliever's fire is already described, joining shown alternatives to destination.
The reminder addresses whoever wills to go straight, turning response into an act of directed movement.
The next ayah locates that willing within the will of God, bounding the traveler's choice without erasing it.
The messenger asks no payment, only that whoever wills take a road toward his Lord.
The warning is a reminder from which whoever wills may take a road toward the Lord.
The true Day is announced and the listener is invited to take a place of return toward the Lord, joining route and final return.
The command not to serve Satan identifies one allegiance as an enemy-led course.
The command to serve God names that worship as a straight road, completing the two-allegiance scene of 36:60.
The change of direction distinguishes one who follows the messenger from one who turns on his heels, using the source root's bodily retreat in a guidance test.
The question whether believers will turn back on their heels if the messenger dies turns spiritual retreat into the exact bodily motion developed beside the pass.
People who heard God's signs are described as recoiling on their heels, making retreat follow disclosed speech rather than ignorance.
Those who turn back after guidance has become clear enact the section's heel-turn after a route has been shown.
Leaders guide by God's command when they exercise patience and certainty, joining the guide who goes before with the endurance required on the way.
The believing man asks his people to follow him so he may guide them to the way of right, explicitly putting a guide in front of travelers.
He contrasts the passing enjoyment of the nearer life with the lasting abode of the Hereafter, explaining the destination of his offered way.
Abraham asks his father to follow him so that he may guide him on an even road, closely matching the guide who advances before the traveler.
The ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy to be followed than one who cannot guide without first being guided.
God commands Moses to lead the servants by night and strike out a dry road through the sea without fear, joining advance, staff-mediated passage, and reassurance.
Moses' staff opens the sea and leaves each parted side like a tremendous mountain, forming a traversable corridor between two raised walls.
The disbelievers spend wealth to block God's road, then their spending becomes regret and ends in defeat and gathering to Hell; expenditure, obstruction, and outcome form one chain.
People are called to spend, yet some are miserly; the ayah says their refusal harms themselves, directly staging the call and non-action at the pass.
When told to set out, some cling heavily to the earth and prefer near life, a bodily refusal to rise and move.
The command to set out light or heavy and strive with wealth and selves supplies both bodily advance and costly expenditure.
Those who sit back without disability are distinguished from those who strive with wealth and body, closely matching the contrast between immobility and undertaking the difficult act.
One who worships on an edge turns away when trial strikes, combining precarious terrain, testing, and retreat.
Misguidance is pictured as a constricted chest like someone painfully climbing into the sky, a direct bodily image of ascent, distress, and guidance.
The community had stood on the lip of a pit of fire and God rescued it, supplying the precipice beside the route and the opposite of falling into it.
A foundation on the edge of a collapsing cliff gives way with its builder into Hellfire, making moral construction terminate in a literal downward plunge.
God's feeding against hunger states the provision that the travelers themselves are required to mediate on a day of hunger.
A secure, well-provisioned town that rejects God's gifts is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing provision into the hardship its ingratitude denied.
The wealthy sign-denier is forced into صَعُودًا, an arduous ascent; the climb he would not choose as moral action returns as imposed punishment.
Whoever turns from the Lord's reminder is made to tread an ascending punishment, reversing refusal of the shown hard way into a compulsory hard ascent.
A crowd plunges into the fire with its leaders using the other Quranic form of the section's اقتحم root; the unmade plunge at the saving pass becomes a plunge into punishment.
Hell is the evil resting place into which the damned enter, supplying the destination for the plunging crowd of 38:59.
The person with light scales has an abyss as his destination; its هَاوِيَةٌ uses the falling root found in the dictionary definition of blind plunging.
Those who conceal scripture for a small price consume only fire, turning withheld guidance and purchased wealth into inward fire.
They exchange guidance for error and are described as astonishingly enduring toward fire, the section's explicit reversal of saving patience.
Pharaoh goes before his people on Judgment Day and leads them into fire, an exact dark reversal of the guide named for preceding those he guides.
The command to guide the wrongdoers onto the road of Hell uses guidance and a road for the punitive opposite destination.
Leaders who call people toward fire reverse the good guide's forward position and reveal where false leadership ends.
The condemned say their masters and great ones led them away from the road, showing guidance's social form turned into misdirection.
God could have raised the sign-bearer, but he clung to the earth and followed desire; chosen low attachment replaces possible elevation.
Those left behind rejoice at sitting, dislike exertion with wealth and body, and cite the heat; the answer that Hell is hotter makes avoided strain return as fire.
The weak, sick, and those lacking means are exempt when sincere, marking bodily inability as a real boundary distinct from willful refusal.
Those who cannot find mounts turn back weeping because they lack means, a compassionate reversal of heel-turning through reluctance.
God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, setting a limit around the section's claim that the pass demands real exertion.
The command to strive fully is paired with the assurance that no constriction has been placed in religion, bounding moral difficulty against pointless impossibility.
Humans and jinn are challenged to pass beyond the regions of heaven and earth but told they cannot penetrate without authority, illuminating the source's language of passage and no exit.
Moses and his servant deliberately retrace their footsteps to recover the sought place; turning back on a route here repairs an omission rather than abandons guidance.
An easy gain and short journey would have drawn the laggards, but the long distance deterred them, exposing refusal that appears specifically when the road is hard.
Those left behind claim that wealth and families occupied them, making worldly holdings the stated reason the body did not advance.
The former laggards are called toward a formidable people and given reward for obedience or punishment for another turn away, renewing the test of advance.
Blindness, lameness, and sickness remove blame, again separating inability to travel from refusal after the route is known.
God creates the human and makes the way easy; if السَّبِيل refers to birth or life's course, it supplies a deliberate counterpoint to the later chosen hard crossing.
God creates and proportionately fashions, providing the making of a creature fit for the route before guidance is mentioned.
God measures and then guides, joining creaturely fitting and direction in the same sequence as created humanity and the shown ridges.
Moses describes the Lord as the One who gave each thing its created form and then guided it, a general formulation of creation followed by direction.
Visible settlements and measured stages make a safe journey possible, presenting a route whose provision and distances have already been arranged.
The people ask that their journeys be lengthened and thereby wrong themselves, turning a furnished road into dispersal and ruin.
Moses names bodily fatigue from the journey; it specifically echoes the section's exhausted traveler, though this journey is not itself the moral pass.
Affluent men ask permission to remain with those who sit when commanded to believe and strive, giving the lagging image a social form.
Their contentment with those left behind fixes the refusal of 9:86 as chosen immobility rather than inability.
Blame falls on wealthy people who ask leave to remain behind, tying capacity and possessions to refused advance.
Disbelief, obstruction of God's road, and opposition after guidance has become clear again make post-guidance resistance the issue.
Opposing the messenger after guidance is clear and following a road other than the believers' road is a direct, if abstract, version of choosing the other visible route.
God does not let a guided people stray until He has clarified what they must avoid, supporting the section's insistence on disclosure before culpable failure.
Guidance has come from the Lord, yet people follow conjecture and desire, another instance of preference overriding supplied direction.
Those who threaten from every road and divert people from God's way are told to inspect the corrupters' outcome, joining road obstruction to road-end.
The command to travel through the earth and inspect the deniers' outcome makes عاقبة a road's observable end in the source section's secondary sense.
Travel through the earth is again ordered so the deniers' outcome may be seen, concretizing result as the terminus of a journey.
After messengers call every community to serve God and avoid false gods, travel reveals the deniers' outcome, joining disclosed alternatives and their end.
Travel and inspection of the criminals' outcome turn the source root's abstract recompense back into a route and its terminus.
The listener must travel through the earth and see the earlier associators' outcome, a repeated Quranic enactment of road-to-end.
Travel reveals the outcome of people stronger than the present deniers, placing physical strength under the judgment of the road's end.
Travel shows the outcome of earlier peoples whose greater power and earthly traces did not save them.
The journey to former peoples' outcome shows that numbers, strength, traces, and earnings could not avail them, answering the source's confidence in wealth and power.
Travel discloses the end of earlier peoples whom God destroyed, linking the road's عاقبة to the destruction sense developed beside it.
The warning that people will learn who possesses the outcome of the abode makes recompense the final ownership of a route, though no physical road is staged.
The final abode is for those who seek neither elevation nor corruption on earth, and the outcome belongs to the wary; worldly height is bounded by the true end.
Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, giving moral work a vertical movement that complements the bodily ascent of the pass.
Seeking help through patience and prayer is described as weighty except for the humble, identifying a saving practice that itself feels difficult.
People are not left merely to say they believe without being tested, denying arrival by verbal claim alone.
Testing earlier peoples distinguishes truthful travelers from liars, giving the hardship in 29:2 its revelatory purpose.
Testing in wealth and persons is paired with patience and taqwa as matters of resolve, connecting expenditure, hardship, and endurance.
Broad mountain roads across the spread earth may faintly illuminate the source's rugged pass by contrast; the ayah concerns ordinary travel, so the moral bridge remains uncertain.
God creates the human from a mixed drop in order to test him, supplying the creation-and-trial premise immediately before the shown road of 76:3.
God states that ease is present with hardship, directly qualifying what the difficult pass contains rather than promising a life without difficulty.
The repeated assurance that ease accompanies hardship makes the relation emphatic and therefore contributes independently to the section's difficult-road scene.
When one task is finished, the addressee is commanded to rise into further exertion, turning received ease into purposeful new labor.
The exertion of 94:7 is given an upward destination by directing longing toward the Lord.
The blazing fire is warned as the far end of the withholding course described earlier in the surah.
Entry into that fire is assigned to the most wretched, making the wrong course terminate in bodily arrival.
Denial and turning away identify the refusal that carries the traveler to the fire of 92:14-15.
The most wary person is kept distant from the fire, opening the opposite outcome to the denier who turned away.
The person spared from fire gives wealth in order to purify himself, directly linking expenditure to the saving branch.
Seeking the face of the Most High supplies the same Godward intention that accompanies patient spending in 13:22.
Final satisfaction completes the outcome of the giver's course.
Receiving the record in the right hand opens the successful outcome after every person's labor toward the Lord in 84:6.
The right-hand traveler receives an easy reckoning, joining exertion on the way to ease at the end.
Joyful return to one's people gives the successful laborer a reached homecoming.
Receiving the record behind the back opens the opposed outcome and gives retreating bodily orientation to it.
The failed traveler calls for destruction when confronted with his result.
He enters a blazing fire, supplying the terminal destination of the backward-oriented branch.
God identifies His straight road and commands people to follow it rather than the other roads that divide them away from it.
The messenger is told that revelation enables him to guide people toward a straight road, placing a human guide before the travelers.
The next ayah identifies that straight road as God's road and places the whole journey under God's final return.
Right direction has become distinct from error, and choosing it is pictured as taking hold of an unbreakable handhold; disclosure must be followed by bodily commitment.
The messenger is commanded to hold fast to revelation because he is upon a straight road, joining firmness of grip to correct direction.
One blind in this life is still blinder in the Hereafter and farther astray from the road, connecting unused perception to failed direction.
As Moses physically turns toward Midian, he hopes that his Lord will guide him to the even road, joining actual travel and divine guidance.
A man runs from the far end of the city and urges his people to follow the messengers, embodying urgent forward response to guidance.
He commands them to follow guides who ask no payment and are themselves guided, clarifying whom the running man follows.
Moses commands his people to enter the assigned land and not turn back on their rear sides lest they become losers.
The people cite the land's formidable inhabitants and refuse entry until the obstacle removes itself, a direct refusal before a difficult crossing.
Two God-fearing men tell them to enter through the gate and promise that committed entry will bring victory.
The people answer that Moses and his Lord should fight while they remain sitting, making bodily non-action explicit.
Their refused entry ends in forty years of forbidden arrival and wandering through the land, an aimless hardship produced by avoiding the purposeful one.
Believers are warned that obeying the disbelievers will turn them back on their heels and return them as losers.
Believers are commanded to seek help through patience and prayer and assured that God is with the patient, repeating the support named for the difficult crossing.
The Prophet must urge believers into the hard encounter, and patient endurance is said to overcome far greater numbers.
God's testing makes the strivers and the patient manifest, joining difficult action to the endurance that sustains it.
Wealth spent in God's road grows like a seed into many ears, reversing the boast that expenditure simply annihilates piled wealth.
Satan's promise of poverty explains how fear blocks expenditure, while God's promise of forgiveness and bounty discloses the other end.
Open charity is good and hidden giving to the poor is better, directly repeating the public-and-secret expenditure joined to patience in 13:22.
The deserving poor are constrained in God's road and unable to travel the earth, joining bodily restriction and hidden need to the giver's obligation.
Family, accumulated wealth, trade, and homes are set against striving with wealth and body; attachment to possessions can stop the traveler.
Hoarded gold and silver and failure to spend on God's road receive a warning of painful punishment.
The hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, making withheld wealth return bodily as fire.
Those who refuse to set out are threatened with painful punishment and replacement, giving the earth-clinging refusal of 9:38 its end.
Believers exchange their lives and wealth for the Garden, making bodily risk and expenditure the price of the reached abode.
Giving relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due specifies where wealth must move rather than be held or wasted.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit, giving bodily form to the boundary between miserliness and ruinous expenditure.
Owners are commanded to contract for emancipation when good is known in the enslaved and to give them from God's wealth, concretely joining freeing to expenditure.
Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due is called better for those who seek God's face, echoing both the pass's recipients and Godward intent.
The righteous recognize in their wealth a right for the asker and the deprived, repeating the distribution that reverses withholding.
A saving transaction is announced, framing the next ayah's costly action as a route out of painful punishment.
Faith and striving with wealth and body are the saving transaction, combining material expenditure and personal exertion.
Forgiveness and gardens are the reached return of that expenditure and effort.
People are told to spend before death arrives and makes the refuser wish for delay so that he could give charity and become righteous.
Humans are told to walk the earth's shoulders, eat God's provision, and remember the resurrection to Him, joining raised terrain, sustenance, travel, and end.
God makes the earth traversable and places roads in it so people may be guided, another literal road furnished before travel.
Travel through the earth should produce understanding hearts and hearing ears; the ayah insists that the decisive blindness is inward, not lack of physical eyes.
God recognizes bodily limits, illness, travel, and struggle, then lightens the imposed exertion while retaining prayer and expenditure.
The migrant finds many refuges and spaciousness on the road, and even death after setting out leaves his reward secured with God.
The human is created in the finest stature, establishing the bodily height from which the two outcomes that follow diverge.
The human is then returned to the lowest of the low, a vertical reversal of the possible ascent.
Faith and good action are excepted from that descent and receive an unending reward.
People prefer the nearer life, naming the choice of immediate ease that can block the harder saving course.
The Hereafter is declared better and more lasting, giving the preferred near life its true comparison and end.
For the person who exercises taqwa, God makes an exit, directly answering the section's image of a difficulty through which a way must be found.
Unexpected provision, divine sufficiency, and a measure fixed for everything supply what the traveler cannot see in advance.
Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge but is reminded that God destroyed people stronger and more numerous than he.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, giving arrogant wealth an emphatic downward end with no helpers.
Those who had desired his position recognize that provision is expanded or constrained by God and that deniers do not succeed.
The ruined owner turns his palms over what he spent while his garden lies fallen on its trellises, joining expenditure, destruction, and downward collapse.
The final outcome of Satan and the person he misleads is that both remain in fire, pairing a false caller with the road's disastrous عاقبة.
Those who prefer near life bar people from God's road and seek to make it crooked, combining wrong preference with active deformation of the route.
Wrongdoers obstruct God's road and seek it crooked while denying the Hereafter, linking route obstruction to denial of its end.
God lets the works of those who disbelieve and obstruct His road go astray, making their attempted road-block rebound upon their own deeds.
Disbelief and obstruction of God's road are themselves described as straying far, turning the blockers into lost travelers.
Those who disbelieve and obstruct God's road receive added punishment for their corruption, supplying the obstruction's destination.
Receiving the record in the right hand opens the fortunate branch of the same passage that later exposes useless wealth and neglected feeding.
Receiving the record in the left hand opens the branch whose owner will confess that wealth failed and the poor were not fed.
The failed person is seized and bound, beginning the compulsory bodily movement toward punishment.
He is thrust into Hellfire, giving the non-feeder's course a physical destination.
He is then inserted into a long chain, intensifying the contrast between saving self-restraint and punitive confinement.
Those who break covenant, sever what God commands joined, and corrupt the earth receive the curse and the bad abode, the opposed continuation to 13:22-24.
The companions of the right are named as one final group, repeating the two-sided human outcome that stands after the pass.
The companions of the left are named as the opposed final group.
Competitive accumulation distracts people, identifying wealth itself as the force that diverts them from the costly good.
The distraction persists until the accumulators reach the graves, abruptly placing hoarded increase against the journey's end.
In encirclement, eyes swerve and hearts reach throats, supplying the bodily panic from which patience must hold the self.
Believers are tested and violently shaken in that position, a concrete instance of entering the middle of frightening hardship.
The garden owners explicitly resolve that no poor person will enter their crop that day, staging deliberate withholding of food.
After the garden's destruction, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived, making withheld provision return as deprivation.
The command to spend on God's road is paired with a prohibition against throwing oneself into destruction, marking the boundary between courageous expenditure and blind self-ruin.
Associating partners with God is likened to falling from the sky and being snatched or cast far away, supplying the downward opposite of the saving ascent.
No mountain can shelter Noah's son from God's decree; physical height cannot replace entering the offered means of rescue.
Turning blind from the reminder is answered by a satanic companion, showing a case where neglected guidance produces deceptive accompaniment.
Those companions avert people from the road while the people think themselves guided, a boundary case against the section's fully visible refusal.
Pharaoh claims that he guides his people only to the way of right; 40:38 later exposes the same formula in the mouth of the true believing guide.
Whenever the wrongdoers try to leave the fire, they are returned to it, turning avoidance of the saving difficulty into a destination with no exit.
Every attempted escape from the fire's anguish sends its people back into it, a punitive reversal of passing through hardship to freedom.
God lightens the combat burden because of human weakness while still naming patient endurance, setting a measured limit around demanded toughness.
God wishes to lighten the human burden because the human was created weak, bounding chosen exertion by creaturely capacity.
God intends ease rather than hardship in the fasting ordinance, guarding the difficult-road image from implying that hardship is desired for itself.
The transgressors are assigned an evil place of return, introducing the destination that 38:56 names and the plunging crowd of 38:59 enters.
Those who spent and struggled before victory receive a higher degree than later actors, joining timely expenditure to moral elevation.
A good loan to God is promised multiplication and noble reward, another reversal of wealth as merely consumed or lost.
Wealth and children are called a test while the great reward remains with God, placing possessions within the road's trial rather than outside it.
Those who withhold God's bounty wrongly think it good; what they withheld will be collared around them on the final day.
The laggards who avoided the earlier expedition ask to follow once spoils are available, exposing selective willingness when the difficult road becomes profitable.
People possess eyes but do not see with them and are called farther astray, supporting the distinction between furnished perception and actual guidance.
Lot's ruined settlement remains on an established road, making past destruction a visible sign encountered by later travelers.
Travelers pass the destroyed people of Lot in the morning, placing the warning directly on their ordinary route.
They pass the same ruins at night yet are asked whether they will understand, showing repeated visibility without moral response.
Travel reveals earlier peoples of greater strength, cultivation, and building who nevertheless wronged themselves after messengers brought signs.
God makes exemplary people leaders who guide by His command and perform good works, another positive form of the guide who goes before.
Satan turns back on his heels after seeing what the opposing army cannot see; the exact retreat motion appears here in a different, fearful context.
The miserly both withhold and command others to withhold while concealing God's bounty, reversing the travelers' mutual counsel toward generosity.
Believers are asked whether they expect to be left without their striving and loyalties being made known, another denial of untested arrival.
The messenger is commanded to endure like the resolute messengers and not hasten the deniers' end, joining patience to confidence in the coming destination.
Patience is located in God's aid, while grief and constriction over opponents are forbidden, directly answering the bodily distress gathered around the climb.
Rebellious settlements taste the consequence of their conduct, and the عاقبة of their affair is loss, using the road-end root for collective ruin.
The disbelievers will learn who possesses the outcome of the abode, repeating the section's use of عُقْبَى for the final owner of the road's end.

Moses identifies his staff as something he leans on and uses in other ways; it faintly anchors the source dictionary's guiding staff in a Quranic object, though this ayah does not say it probes the road.
Mary and Jesus are lodged on elevated, settled ground with flowing water; the literal raised terrain and provision are specific, but their relation to the difficult two-ridge choice is indirect.
